title: One action at a time
hook: build your life action by action; no one can stop you doing each well (Meditations 8.32)
tomorrow: Not the whole life at once

segments.voice: Yesterday: matter, act, meaning, and the sting about being good tomorrow instead of today. Your line was what it means. What did you do with its meaning in mind? Day six hundred one.

A stone wall on an old farm. No mortar, no blueprint. Somebody built it by picking up one stone, turning it until it fit, setting it down, and picking up the next. When a stone was too big, they didn't quit. They set it aside and found another that fit the gap. Generations later, the wall still stands. Marcus Aurelius thought a life gets built the same way. The title of this part of the path comes from today's entry.
screen: `A DRY STONE WALL.` → `ONE STONE, THEN THE NEXT.` → `A LIFE BUILT THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the building. In Meditations eight, thirty-two, Marcus says you have to put your life together action by action. And if each action does its job as far as it can, be satisfied. Not each life. Each action. That's the unit. Second, the promise. Then he says something bold: no one can stop you from making each action do its job. Someone might object, he imagines, that some outside thing will get in the way. Marcus answers: nothing can stop you acting justly, with self-control, and with good sense. The world can block your plans. It can't block the way you meet the block. Third, the stone that doesn't fit. Then the most practical part. Maybe, he says, something will stop you doing the particular action you intended. Fine. Accept the obstacle gracefully, turn to what is possible, and a new action takes its place, one that fits the same building. That's the farmer setting aside the stone that's too big and finding one that fits. The wall keeps rising. Fourth, why this frees you. If your life is one giant project, every setback threatens the whole thing. If it's built action by action, a setback is just one stone that didn't fit. The next stone is always available. You don't need to fix your whole life today. You need to do the next action well. Then the next. Marcus wrote it for an emperor's days. It fits a stack of laundry just as well.
screen: `BUILD YOUR LIFE ACTION BY ACTION.` · `NO ONE CAN STOP YOU ACTING WELL.` · `BLOCKED? A NEW ACTION FITS.` · `THE NEXT STONE IS ALWAYS THERE.` · then, large: `ONE ACTION AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Don't think about your whole life, or even your whole day. Just ask: what is the very next action I'll take after this sit? Standing up? Making a call? Washing a cup? See it clearly. Then picture doing that one action well, with care. Nothing else. If your mind jumps ahead to the rest of the list, set the list down and come back to the next stone. The bell holds the time.
Marcus, who said a life is put together action by action, and when one is blocked, another that fits takes its place. Today's word.
Your line: pick up the next stone. Today, when something blocks your plan, accept it, and do the next possible action well. Day six hundred one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often treat their day as a series of single actions to do well, and when a plan is blocked, they accept it and choose the next possible action rather than abandoning the whole.

trapdoor: what you thought: take it one step at a time.
what it means: a life is built of single actions; no one can stop you doing each one well, and a blocked one can be replaced by another that fits.
what a scholar hears: 8.32 applies the Stoic 'reserve clause': you aim at an action 'if nothing prevents,' so an obstacle redirects you instead of defeating you.

notes: Meditations 8.32 paraphrased: build up life action by action, content if each fulfills its duty as far as possible; no one can hinder this; something external may stand in the way, but nothing hinders acting justly, soberly and wisely; if some action is hindered, accept it and pass to what is allowed, and another action takes its place that fits the composition. Confirm.
The 'reserve clause' (hupexhairesis) framing in the trapdoor is interpretive; confirm that 8.32 is fairly read this way.
'Practice' from praxis: confirm etymology (via Greek praktikos and Latin practica).
The part title ('one action at a time') is this path's label, drawn from 8.32.
Reviewer softened the claim that Marcus wrote this while running an empire at war: where and when book 8 was written is unknown; the line now refers only to the wars and plague of his reign. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the invented 'two hundred years' figure, the remaining claim that Marcus wrote 8.32 'while carrying an empire through years of war and plague' (still a dating claim, and it repeated day 602's hook), and the etymology in the original note.
